newsitem.title: GERMANY: Goldman Sachs says EMU "most likely" starts in '99.
newsitem.headline: Goldman Sachs says EMU "most likely" starts in '99.

text.p: Goldman Sachs economists reconfirmed on Thursday their bank's view that European economic and monetary union (EMU) will likely start on time despite risks of slow economic growth.

"We do think that the most likely event is that a start date of 1999 does get met," Gavyn Davies, chief international economist for Goldman Sachs International told a conference organised by Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt.
He said the forecast assumed seven to eight countries would be able to participate in the first round of EMU, scheduled for 1999.

However, Davies said such a scenario was "very, very dependent on the growth rate in gross domestic product (GDP)" in the major European countries, noting that even a slight deviation from currently-forecast rates could make a delay unavoidable.
The U.S. investment bank predicted German and French GDP growth near 2.25 percent in 1997.
"If the figures come in any lower than that, we shall a significant problem in getting anywhere (near) the Maastricht criteria (for EMU entry)," Davies said.

Goldman estimates that a one-percentage point shortfall in its GDP growth forecasts would leave both Germany and France with public deficits of about four percent of GDP, significantly above the three-percent figure specified in Maastricht.

Davies said the requirements to meet the Maastricht criteria by the end of this year meant that if GDP growth slowed, there was very little that could be done either through fiscal or monetary policy to redress the situation.
But Thomas Mayer, senior economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt, said he believed Germany would "find a way" to consolidate its public finances sufficiently to qualify.
